questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I have always wanted to try living in Italy. My family and I have been coming there my whole life and I have studied the Italian language for a long time. I wished to try living la dolce vita in Bella Italia. 
Apart from that, I saw it as a good opportunity to get the Erasmus grant as support, so I didn't suck dry my savings.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: That was difficult. You definitely need to seek out all information yourself and find out who you can email your questions to. It puts a lot of responsibility, time and work on yourself, when you go to Milan on exchange. But to some degree I think that concerns going on exchange in general.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There is an Erasmus office with a coordinator, Massimo Costa, who is good at responding fast to emails. But the academic assistance was almost non-existing. I found it really hard to make it all add up and I had to figure it all out myself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It wasn't easy and a lot of options were expensive. A lot find a room in a common apartment sharing it with quite a few other students (strangers), but from what I heard that is a mixed experience because people don't take any responsibility to clean common areas properly. 
I found my first apartment via the website Italianway, which I was overall very satisfied with. I found a big apartment really close to my campus. I needed 3 roommates for that, so I wrote a Facebook post searching for roommates in a Facebook group made for all students from University of Copenhagen going to Milan that semester. I ended up sharing that apartment with 3 other girls from UCPH. However we could not stay there for the whole semester. 
The next apartment I found via Housinganywhere but actually we just took over from some other girls from UCPH who were going home earlier than expected. Also a nice big apartment, where I found a german girl to join me and my friend. I found her by writing a text in an Erasmus whatsapp groupchat.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It can be quite expensive but on the other hand you live in the city, which is cool. I paid 4500kr per month for the first apartment, which was unusually cheap. And 7500kr per month for the other apartment. But I have friends who have paid between 6000-10.000 per month during their stay. 
There are a few university dorms that you can apply for. They are a lot cheaper but the rooms are small and the place is generally pretty dirty. Pros and cons.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I felt pretty lucky but I also put a lot of work into finding some good places, so I had some really good experiences with beautiful big apartments and living with roomies I chose myself and hit it off with really well. And I never got lonely because I lived with roomies and I made new friends as I didn't know them before going on exchange.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I can't even remember it now. But it was quite a bit of work to make it all up and figure out how to take courses on different master programmes to make it add up and how I made sure that it didn't overlap too much.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up with some courses that covered topics that I was very interested in, so I guess it added up fine. But also a lot of complications and not a lot of options that could work out.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Explore the unimi website and look in the course catalogue and look at the class schedule to see if it overlaps. Ally yourself with someone else if you can and figure it out together.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I honestly wouldn't recommend Molecular Biomedicine students to go on exchange to Milan. The academic options are very limited and I did not like their method of teaching and chaotic exams and unhelpful professors that are hard to understand due to accent. But I have a feeling it was way easier on the other faculties. I had friends studying law, HR etc that had a very easy time and enjoyed the academics more. But the teaching, lectures and exams at the molecular biology/medicine/biotechnology faculties were very hard compared to everything else.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Specifically my courses were pretty hard because of everything described so far. 
But students at other faculties said it was way easier than what they were used to at home.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
No curriculum in books, only slides for studying. 
Very dry lectures, not much class interaction.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Communicable and non-communicable diseases 
Pathogenetic basis of disease
Applied pharmacology to biotechnology
Italian language course

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Pathogenetic basis of disease. 
I enjoyed this class. A lot of pathologic basis of different diseases. A big course with 12 ECTS but only a multiple choice exam. It was interesting. 
Communicable and non-communicable diseases had the most interesting topics, but this is a no-go recommendation, as it has two parts and two exams and the professor responsible for the first part is super intimidating and unhelpful and arrogant and failed everyone including me at the exam. 
Italian language course could have so much potential and I was looking forward to it but unfortunately in was online on microsoft teams and it is impossible to learn that way.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Cannot think of anything.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transport is super cheap and their public transport system is amazing with perfect metro lines, the beautiful tram and busses. A travel card with a monthly subscription was only around 20 euros a month, so super cheap. 
I made sure to take advantage of cappucinos for the general price of 1,5 euros and cocktails and wine for 3-7 euros. Eating out is also cheap, so we did that a lot. Grocery shopping is not that much cheaper, but still some! Especially veggies and fruit.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Huge Erasmus student network in Italy! I was sure that I was gonna take advantage of that and spend a lot of time on that but I ended up finding friends through school and also a lot of danish students from UCPH that I hung out with instead. But a lot of fun social events and opportunities to meet new friends through ESN.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Bologna is beautiful and centro storico there is classic italy vibes, so cozy. 
I wish I could have taken a trip to the dolomites and done some hiking. But como and the other lakes are also beautiful when the weather is nice. The old town in Bergamo is also breathtaking at golden hour.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I felt at home pretty fast.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: All the academic differences for sure.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Their way of enjoying life.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Go down to Italy before school starts. It starts super late in late september/early october, so I wish I had enjoyed some summer time there and done some traveling before school started. Because time goes fast and then there are exams already in december. 
2. You have to be patient and not stress about all the practical and academic stuff, because the italians don't stress. Things are confusing and takes time.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Maybe learn a bit of Italian before? Not all italians speak english and they can be rude because they feel insecure when trying to speak english.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to feel at home in another country. When I came back to Milan after Christmas, I had a strong feeling of feeling at home when people spoke Italian around me. The weather, the going out culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The academics and the exams. I had a rough time getting through that in december and january.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
